2008-10-20 · law change. Ecuador's 1998 constitution had granted the Banco Central del Ecuador independence. The constitution that replaced it, sponsored by Rafael Correa's government and published in the Registro Oficial on 20 October 2008, removed it. Article 303 states that the drafting of monetary, credit, foreign exchange and financial policy is the exclusive power of the Executive, to be implemented through the Central Bank, and that the Central Bank is a public-law entity whose organisation and operation are set by law. The bank was left as the body that carries out policy rather than the body that makes it: its own website describes its role as implementing the policies formulated by the Executive under article 303. The monetary board was replaced by a central bank board of five members appointed by the president and confirmed by Congress. The academic monetary and fiscal history of Ecuador prepared for the University of Chicago's series lists 2008 as the suppression of central bank independence, alongside the suppression of the fiscal stabilisation funds, and states that the constitution removed the bank's autonomy and made it dependent on the executive branch, which became responsible for designing fiscal and monetary policy. The change was structural rather than an episode with an end: Ecuador has been dollarised since 2000, so the bank had no currency of its own to run, and article 303 remains in force. The Monetary and Fiscal History of Ecuador, 1960-2017 (Cueva and Diaz, University of Chicago Becker Friedman Institute)

2020-2021 · conflict of interest / paid outside directorship · alleged. A Global Witness investigation published on 19 February 2021 found that senior Central Bank of Libya officials hold paid overseas directorships, and that Governor Saddek Elkaber chairs a London-based bank indirectly owned by the Central Bank of Libya, which the report calls a conflict of interest. The report also said the bank's letters of credit data point to ongoing financial crime in the system, citing nearly $2.5bn of private sector letters of credit approved between April and July 2020 and a $110m letter of credit for power equipment diverted to a UAE company with a near identical name to the original contractor. The report states it makes no allegation that any individual or bank broke the law. Discredited (Global Witness)
2020 · conflict of interest · alleged. Global Witness reported that most Libyan letters of credit enter the international system through ABC International Bank in London, a commercial bank indirectly owned by the central bank and chaired by Governor Saddek Elkaber. It called this a clear conflict of interest, given his authority over letters of credit and anti-money-laundering rules. It built a database of nearly $2.5bn of letters of credit over 13 weeks in 2020 and said sources described mispricing, laundering and procurement fraud; the page reports no official finding of fraud. Global Witness reveals fraudulent Libyan Letters of Credit money entering international financial system via London (Global Witness)
2013-2023 · theft or fraud · convicted. The Misrata Criminal Court convicted two people of belonging to an organization set up to seize US$128 million and €5 million from the central bank's Sirte branch in 2013 through coercion. One got 15 years in prison and a LD 2.5 million fine; the other got 13 years and a LD 50,000 fine. The Attorney General's Office reported the ruling in October 2023. Two convicted for stealing Central Bank of Libya funds worth over US$ 128 million (Libya Herald)

The Associated Press, carried by ABC News, reported that Libya's Tripoli-based presidential council, allied with Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah's government, issued a decree firing Sadiq al-Kabir as governor of the Central Bank of Libya. Al-Kabir had led the bank since October 2011. The council named Mohamed Abdul Salam al-Shukri, an economist and former deputy governor, to replace him. The report says the decree was issued late on a Sunday and gives no official reason for the firing. The dispute was over who has the authority to appoint the governor: the east-based House of Representatives and the Supreme Council of State, both of which are mandated to appoint central bank governors under the constitutional document, called the firing illegitimate. The IMF AREAER 2023 classification (end-April 2023) lists Ecuador, El Salvador, Marshall Islands, Micronesia, Palau, Panama and Timor-Leste as having no separate legal tender with the US dollar as anchor.
Ecuador adopted the US dollar in January 2000 at 25,000 sucres per dollar under the Ley para la Transformación Económica (Registro Oficial Suplemento 34, 13 March 2000); Article 94 of the Código Orgánico Monetario y Financiero (2014) makes the dollar the currency of transactions.
In El Salvador, legal reforms made private-sector acceptance of Bitcoin voluntary and tax payments payable only in US dollars, listed as prior actions for the IMF EFF approved on 26 February 2025.
